questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{t-1}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=2.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =2+{\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{[{e}^{t-1}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2+({e}^{2-1}-{e}^{1-1}) \\  & =2+({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2+e-1 \\  & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=e+1.$

The graph above shows the velocity of an object moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis. At time $t=2$ the particle is located at the position $x=4.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=6?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=6$ is equal to its position at $t=2$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [2,6].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(6)=x(2)+{\int }_{2}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(2)=4$, and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{2}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=2$ to $t=6.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{2}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t=4.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(6)=4+4=8.
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=6$ is $x=8.$

questions.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)={sec}^{2}⁡(t).$ At time $t=0$ the particle is located at the position $x=-2.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\frac{\pi }{4})=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-2+{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2+{[\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-2+\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0) \\  & =-2+1-0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is $x=-1.$
